Theme

Latin word

fidēs

fidēs, fideī f.

noun, fifth declension

credit, the trust that lending rests on; faith, trust; a stringed instrument, lyre; one’s word, pledge, good faith

In this lexicon

  • economy

    also used · classical · Cic. Imp. Pomp. 19: fidem concidisse, credit had collapsed; Caes. BC 3.1.2: cum fidēs tōtā Ītaliā esset angustior

  • faith

    the recommended word · classical · Traupman 152, 312; Vulg. Mc. 5.34; Lact. 4.30 (Lewis & Short)

  • lyre

    also used · classical

  • word

    the recommended word · classical · Cic. Off. 1.39: fidem hostī datam fallere; Cic. Off. 1.23: fundāmentum autem est jūstitiae fidēs; Traupman p. 111: fidem dare (frangere, servāre)

  • fidēs majōrēs: cello

    Renaissance

  • fidēs crūrālēs: cello

    modern

  • fidēs statāria: double bass

    modern

Examples

  • haec fidēs atque haec ratiō pecūniārum, quae Rōmae, quae in forō versātur, implicāta est cum illīs pecūniīs Asiāticīs et cohaeret

    this credit, this whole system of money that operates at Rome and in the Forum, is bound up with that money in Asia and hangs together with itCic. Imp. Pomp. 19

    In the entry for economy

  • cum fidēs tōtā Ītaliā esset angustior neque crēditae pecūniae solverentur

    since credit was tighter all over Italy and loans were not being repaidCaes. BC 3.1.2

    In the entry for economy

  • Fīlia, fidēs tua tē salvam fēcit: vāde in pāce

    Daughter, your faith has made you well: go in peaceVulg. Mc. 5.34

    In the entry for faith

  • Chrīstusque nōbīs sit cibus, pōtusque noster sit fidēs

    let Christ be our food, and faith our drinkAmbr. hymn. Splendor 21–22

    In the entry for faith

  • Modicae fideī, quārē dubitāstī?

    You of little faith, why did you doubt?Vulg. Mt. 14.31

    In the entry for faith

  • ad supplicium redīre māluit quam fidem hostī datam fallere

    he chose to go back to be put to death rather than break the word he had given the enemyCic. Off. 1.39

    In the entry for word

  • fundāmentum autem est jūstitiae fidēs, id est dictōrum conventōrumque cōnstantia et vēritās

    and the foundation of justice is good faith: that is, standing by what has been said and agreed, and being true to itCic. Off. 1.23
